deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no derivation, formula or computation. It has three components.

(1) Faint brown ink text, upright and right-reading, covering roughly the upper half. Several lines are cancelled with heavier horizontal strokes. As far as it can be made out, it matches the draft letter on the facing page (122r). That letter, dated Göttingen, 5 October 1861, is Riemann's draft to a colleague declining to sign the jointly drafted report on the proposed Central European arc measurement (mitteleuropäische Gradmessung). In this image I can make out an opening that seems to begin 'Nach reiflicher Erwägung …', a closing near the middle reading 'Göttingen, den 5. Octo[ber]' followed by '1861', and a further line below. The cancelled lines line up with the deleted passages of that draft. I read this text as offset or bleed-through from 122r rather than an independent text. It carries no mathematics.

(2) Pencil sketch in the middle: two nearly parallel, slightly wavy horizontal curves crossing each other. Where they cross, a small semicircle hangs below. A faint vertical pencil line descends from this area. One possible reading is a curved surface or profile with a local bulge or cavity, perhaps a meniscus or drop on a surface, or a local disturbance of a level line. That would fit the geodetic context of the letter (the figure of the Earth). This is my conjecture; there is no label.

(3) Two pencil sketches in the lower half.
- A polygon (a pentagon/hexagon-like outline) cut into triangles and quadrilaterals by lines meeting near an interior point. It looks like a polygon subdivided from a vertex or an interior point, or possibly a perspective view of a polyhedron's corner.
- Two or three adjoining polygonal cells, roughly pentagonal or hexagonal, sharing edges. Small arcs mark the angles at several vertices, and faint additional cells are drawn around them.

The angle arcs suggest interest in the angles meeting at vertices of a polygonal network. Possible contexts include angle sums in a cell decomposition (Euler-type counting), cellular or foam-like partitions, or a net of a polyhedron such as the dodecahedron. Nothing is written beside the figures, so any interpretation is speculative (mine).

In short, the page is a reused sheet: a bleed-through of an administrative letter plus idle or exploratory geometric doodles. There is no reconstructible mathematical argument.
